title: Taurine and proline promote lung tumour growth by co-regulating Azgp1/mTOR signalling pathway

sections.abstract: Accurate metabolic biomarkers for lung cancer prognosis remain scarce but crucial. Taurine and proline, two metabolites, are consistently elevated across various cancer stages in previous studies, hinting at their potential role in disease progression. This study is the first to reveal how these metabolites contribute to poor prognosis. Transcriptomic analysis uncovered that taurine and proline downregulated Zinc-α2-glycoprotein (Azgp1), a gene linked to key metabolic pathways. Additionally, Azgp1 could also significantly affect downstream lipid metabolic pathways in lung cancer. Both taurine and proline influenced lipid metabolism via mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR). When Azgp1 was overexpressed, lung cancer progression slowed significantly, alongside reduced mTOR activity. These findings underscore the pro-cancer role of taurine and proline, highlighting the Azgp1/mTOR axis as a vital, yet overlooked, pathway in lung cancer. This study not only advances our understanding but also identifies new therapeutic avenues.
sections.introduction:
Lung cancer, marked by high mortality rates and exceptionally low 5-year survival, has emerged as the deadliest cancer worldwide 1 , 2 . While recent advancements in treatment strategies have led to a slight increase in overall survival rates for lung cancer patients, the disease continues to pose a significant threat to humanity 3 . Consequently, numerous studies have been conducted, yielding valuable findings that are gradually being incorporated into clinical practice. Accurate diagnosis of lung cancer is crucial, as it allows for the development of effective treatment strategies 4 . Identifying valid biomarkers associated with lung cancer has become a focal point of current research 4 .

Metabolomics offer significant advantages in cancer metabolism and biomarker identification 5 . This approach can reveal extensive information about cellular metabolic processes involved in tumour progression 6 . Furthermore, as the end products of various biological processes, metabolites can serve as precise biomarkers reflecting upstream events, such as gene mutations and environmental changes 7 . Changes in metabolites and their pathways can enhance our understanding of metabolic disorders in tumourigenesis and progression 8 . However, metabolomics alone is insufficient for identifying novel metabolic markers and elucidating the related in vivo mechanisms. Fortunately, transcriptomics, a large-scale study of RNA molecules, facilitates a better understanding of numerous molecular underpinnings and biological processes in cancer 9 . Transcriptomics applications provide vital insights into the aetiology and pathogenesis of certain cancers, ultimately benefiting clinical research 10 . Additionally, different omics can reflect biomarker status from gene transcription to metabolism at various levels and enable data complementation. Integrating metabolomic profiling with transcriptomic data is a valuable approach for comprehensively understanding the regulatory processes behind various physiological biomarker phenomena 11 .

Our previous clinical tests successfully identified five valid biomarkers including proline, L-kynurenine, spermidine, taurine, and palmitoyl-L-carnitine, displaying high abundance in the plasma of 110 Chinese patients with lung cancer classified as adenocarcinomas ( n = 63), squamous carcinomas ( n = 41), and other histological types ( n = 6), as compared to healthy individuals 12 . We further validated these findings using lung cancer mouse models, establishing the most suitable animal model for metabolomic studies 13 . Intriguingly, the top three biomarkers including proline, L-kynurenine, and taurine have been reported to be associated with certain cancers including lung cancer, breast cancer, and gastric cancer 14 – 17 . However, the role and underlying mechanism of proline, L-kynurenine, and taurine in lung cancer remain unclear. In this study, we aimed to evaluate the impact of the top three biomarkers including proline, L-kynurenine, and taurine on subcutaneous and even orthotopic lung tumour growth. We hypothesised that metabolites and genes may be co-dysregulated within the same biological process in cancer 8 . Accordingly, we obtained and analysed metabolite and transcript profiles of orthotopic lung tumours using ultra-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS/MS) and high-throughput RNA sequencing, respectively. By combining tumour transcriptome and metabolome analyses, we aimed to validate the role and mechanisms of potential diagnostic biomarkers in lung cancer, thereby enhancing the reliability of our results.
sections.methods:
Taurine (purity >98%, CAS NO.107-35-7), proline (purity ≥99%, CAS NO.147-85-3), and L-kynurenine (purity >98%, CAS NO.2922-83-0) were procured from Dalian Meilun Biological Technology Co., Ltd., China. Uridine (purity = 99%, CAS NO.U820334) was obtained from Mu Biotechnology Co., Ltd., China. Sterile single-use syringes (1 cc/ml) were acquired from Terumo Corporation. RPMI DMEM, phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), fetal bovine serum (FBS, Origin: Canada), penicillin, and streptomycin were sourced from Thermo Scientific (San Diego, CA, USA). HPLC-grade methanol, ammonium acetate, and acetic acid were purchased from Merck Company (Darmstadt, Germany) and Sigma-Aldrich (Allentown, PA). Ultra-pure water was generated using a Millipore Milli-Q system (Millipore, Bedford, MA, USA).

Mouse Lewis lung carcinoma (LLC) cells (ATCC, Manassas, VA, USA) were cultured in RPMI DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS, 50 µg/ml penicillin, and 50 µg/ml streptomycin in a humidified atmosphere (37 °C, 5% CO 2 ) 13 .

All of the following animal experiments were performed according to committee-approved protocols and institutional animal care guidelines by Macau (Registration number: A014/DICV/DIS/2019 Date: 29/8/2019; AL007/DICV/SIS/2017, Date: 21/2/2017). Six- to eight-week-old C57 female mice were acclimatised for 1 week. Approximately 5 × 10 5 LLC cells were suspended in 100 μl serum-free medium and then injected subcutaneously into the right flank of the mice. On day 7, when xenografts reached a size of approximately 30 mm 3 , mice were randomly assigned to the model ( n = 5), proline ( n = 5), L-kynurenine ( n = 5), and taurine groups ( n = 5). Mice received daily drug intervention with vehicle (PBS, i.p.), proline (25 mg/kg, i.p.), L-kynurenine (25 mg/kg, i.p.), or taurine (25 mg/kg, i.p.). Mouse weight and tumour size were measured every 3 days using an electronic balance and caliper 13 , 67 – 69 . On the final day of the study, all mice were humanely euthanized using carbon dioxide asphyxiation, and their lungs and other organs were harvested for further analysis.

Mice were randomly assigned to the control group ( n = 10), model group ( n = 11), taurine group ( n = 10), and proline group ( n = 11) according to their mean body weight. In all the in vivo experiments, “control” denotes the untreated group used as a baseline for comparison, while “model” refers to the experimental system or animal used to replicate lung cancer conditions for studying disease progression and therapeutic interventions. Starting on the third day, mice received daily drug intervention with vehicle (PBS), taurine (25 mg/kg, i.p.), or proline (25 mg/kg, i.p.). Mice were weighed regularly, and tumour growth was monitored in real-time using micro-CT 13 , 68 . Ultimately, all mice were euthanized to collect lung tumours for metabolomics analysis 13 , 70 . On the final day of the study, all mice were humanely euthanized using carbon dioxide asphyxiation, and their lungs and other organs were harvested for further analysis.

A subcutaneous tumour-bearing model was established in female C57BL/6 mice of the same age using the same method. When xenografts reached a size of approximately 30 mm 3 , mice were randomly divided into the model ( n = 5), proline ( n = 5), uridine ( n = 5), and proline combined with uridine groups ( n = 5). Mice received daily drug intervention with vehicle (PBS, i.p.), proline (25 mg/kg, i.p.), uridine (100 mg/kg, i.p.), or a combination of proline (25 mg/kg, i.p.) and uridine (100 mg/kg, i.p.). Mouse weight and tumour size were measured every 3 days using an electronic balance and caliper 67 – 69 . On the final day of the study, all mice were humanely euthanized using carbon dioxide asphyxiation, and their lungs and other organs were harvested for further analysis.

Twelve tumour samples were collected from the four groups and processed according to the supplementary methods 1 to obtain the target products for sequencing library construction. An Illumina Novaseq™ 6000 (LC-Bio Technology CO., Ltd., Hangzhou, China) was used for 2 × 150 bp paired-end sequencing (PE150) 65 , 71 . StringTie (version: stringtie-1.3.4d) with default parameters was employed to assemble the mapped reads of each sample. A comprehensive transcriptome was subsequently reconstructed by merging all transcriptomes using the gffcompare software (version: gffcompare-0.9.8). Transcript expression was assessed by StringTie and ballgown, which were also used to determine mRNA expression abundance by calculating FPKM (fragment per kilobase of transcript per million mapped reads) values 72 , 73 . DESeq2 software was applied to analyse differential gene expression between two different groups (and edgeR between two samples). Genes were identified as DEGs if they had a false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05 and an absolute fold change ≥2. Enrichment analysis of Gene Ontology (GO) functions and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathways was conducted to further investigate the regulatory mechanisms of DEGs 74 – 76 . The above RNA-seq data has been deposited in GEO (GSE282449).

RNA-seq data of 1017 lung cancer samples including lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) and lung squamous carcinoma (LUSC) from the cancer genome atlas (TCGA) were downloaded from UCSC XENA database ( https://xenabrowser.net/datapages/ ). The correlation between Azgp1 expression and key genes expression of the taurine and proline metabolism pathway was calculated using spearman correlation analyses. |r| > 0.1 and p < 0.05 were set as the criteria for the significant correlation. Then, the ggplot2 package (v3.5.1, 10.32614/CRAN.package.ggplot2) in R software (R 4.2.2) was used to construct correlation scatter plots 77 , 78 .

Gene set enrichment analysis using software GSEA (v4.3.1) software ( https://www.gsea-msigdb.org/gsea/index.jsp ) was used to analyse the downstream pathways that Azgp1 may regulate in 1017 lung cancer samples from the TCGA. Hallmark database and KEGG pathway database were selected as the Gene sets database. The number of permutations was determined to be 1000, and Pearson algorithm was selected as the metric for ranking genes. Enrichment scores and p value was calculated in default parameters. |NES| > 1, NOM p val < 0.05, FDR q -val < 0.25 were considered to be significant functional pathways 77 , 79 .

The collected samples were thawed on ice, and metabolite were extracted with 50% methanol Buffer. Briefly, 20 μL of sample was extracted with 120 μL of precooled 50% methanol, vortexed for 1 min, and incubated at room temperature for 10 min; the extraction mixture was then stored overnight at −20 °C. After centrifugation at 4000 × g for 20 min, the supernatants were transferred into new 96-well plates. The samples were stored at −80 °C prior to the LC-MS analysis. In addition, pooled QC samples were also prepared by combining 10 μL of each extraction mixture.

All samples were acquired by the LC-MS system followed machine orders. Firstly, all chromatographic separations were performed using a Thermo Scientific UltiMate 3000 HPLC. An ACQUITY UPLC BEH C18 column (100 mm × 2.1 mm, 1.8 µm, Waters, UK) was used for the reversed phase separation. The column oven was maintained at 35 °C. The flow rate was 0.4 ml/min and the mobile phase consisted of solvent A (water, 0.1% formic acid) and solvent B (Acetonitrile, 0.1% formic acid). Gradient elution conditions were set as follows: 0–0.5 min, 5% B; 0.5–7 min, 5% to 100% B; 7–8 min, 100% B; 8–8.1 min, 100% to 5% B; 8.1–10 min, 5% B. The injection volume for each sample was 4 µl.

A high-resolution tandem mass spectrometer TripleTOF6600plus (SCIEX, Framingham, MA, USA) was used to detect metabolites eluted form the column. The Q-TOF was operated in both positive and negative ion modes. The curtain gas was set 30 PSI, Ion source gas1 was set 60 PSI, Ion source gas2 was set 60 PSI, and an interface heater temperature was 650 °C. For positive ion mode, the Ionspray voltage floating were set at 5000 V, respectively. For negative ion mode, the Ionspray voltage floating were set at −4500 V, respectively. The mass spectrometry data were acquired in IDA mode. The TOF mass range was from 60 to 1200 Da. The survey scans were acquired in 150 ms and as many as 12 product ion scans were collected if exceeding a threshold of 100 counts per second (counts/s) and with a 1+ charge-state. Total cycle time was fixed to 0.56 s. Four time bins were summed for each scan at a pulser frequency value of 11 kHz through monitoring of the 40 GHz multichannel TDC detector with four-anode/channel detection. Dynamic exclusion was set for 4 s. During the acquisition, the mass accuracy was calibrated every 20 samples. Furthermore, in order to evaluate the stability of the LC-MS during the whole acquisition, a quality control sample (Pool of all samples) was acquired after every 10 samples.

MS data pretreatments were performed using XCMS software after extracting and quantifying metabolites from tumour samples using UPLC-MS/MS 80 . This included peak picking, peak grouping, retention time correction, second peak grouping, and annotation of isotopes and adducts. LC-MS raw data files were converted into mzXML format and processed by XCMS, CAMERA, and metaX toolbox implemented with R software 65 . Peak data intensities were further pre-processed by metaX. Student’s t tests were conducted to detect differences in metabolite concentrations between two phenotypes. The p value was adjusted for multiple tests using an FDR (Benjamini–Hochberg).

The detailed procedure was reported previously 81 . The following antibodies were used in this experiment: β-Actin (Cell Signalling Technology (CST), #8457), p-mTOR (Santa Cruz, sc-293133), mTOR (CST, #2983), Azgp1 (ZAP) (Santa Cruz, sc-21720). Amersham ImageQuant™ 800 Western blot imaging systems was used to quantify the signal intensity (Cytiva, Japan).

A lentiviral overexpression vector expressing the mouse Azgp1 gene under the control of the EFS promoter was created. The lentivirus was packaged with the overexpression vector and tested for titre to ensure the virus quality met the requirements for subsequent experiments. In cell screening, bacteria, fungus, mycoplasma, and others were screened to ensure the LLC Cell was not contaminated. LLC Cell was transduced by lentivirus, and resistant cells were selected with corresponding antibiotics to obtain stable cell lines, including mouse Azgp1 overexpression stable cell lines and control virus-transfected cell lines. Finally, mouse Azgp1 expression was detected by QPCR in overexpression stably strains and control cell lines.

LLC (wt) and LLC (Azgp1 overexpression) cells were seeded in 96-well microplates (1000 cells/well). After cell adhesion, cells were placed in an incubator at 37 °C for 72 h. Then, 10 μl of 0.5 mg/ml MTT solution was added to each well, and microplates were placed in an incubator at 37 °C for 4 h. Afterward, 100 μl of DMSO was added to dissolve the crystals. Absorbance was recorded with a spectrometer at 570 and 650 nm.

LLC (wt) and LLC (Azgp1 overexpression) cells were seeded in a 6-well plate with 30,000 cells/well. After cell adhesion, the cells were placed in an incubator at 37 °C separately for approximately 72 h. When colonies were obviously formed, 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) was added to each well for 30 min at 4 °C, followed by crystal violet solution for cell staining for at least 30 min. After washing away the crystal violet solution, colonies were photographed.

All data are presented as the mean ± standard deviation or mean ± standard error of the mean. The statistical differences were analysed by one-way ANOVA and t -test using GraphPad Prism 6 (San Diego, CA, USA). p values < 0.05 were considered significantly different.
sections.results:
In cancer research, proline 14 and L-kynurenine 18 , 19 are typically administered in vivo at low doses (5–30 mg/kg), while taurine is used at higher doses, often exceeding 200 mg/kg, due to its physiological abundance and broad therapeutic window. We conducted preliminary dose-ranging studies for taurine (25–400 mg/kg) in our lung cancer model to reconcile these differences and ensure translational relevance. These experiments revealed a dose-dependent effect on tumour progression, with even the lowest dose (25 mg/kg) showing significant activity 20 . To enhance consistency and translational relevance, we standardised the dosage of all three metabolites to 25 mg/kg in our in vivo experiments. This approach ensures physiological relevance while enabling comparative analysis of their effects under controlled conditions. In this study, we developed lung cancer mouse model through the subcutaneous injection of mouse Lewis lung carcinoma (LLC) cells to explore the role of the top three biomarkers, including taurine (Fig. 1A ), proline (Fig. 1B ), and L-kynurenine (Fig. 1C ), on lung cancer progression tumourigenesis (Fig. 1D ). Confirming our previous clinical results and consistent with other reported research, proline significantly promoted subcutaneous tumour growth (Fig. 1F–H ). For the first time, we found that a significant tumour-promoting effect was observed in the taurine group (Fig. 1F–H ). However, in the L-kynurenine supplement group, there was no significant tumour-promoting effect. There were no significant differences in body weight and organ/body ratios among the four groups (Fig. 1E, I ). Our preliminary conclusion showed that an abundance of taurine and proline in vivo could result in a poor prognosis for lung cancer. We previously reported that to achieve better tumour-related metabolism research, the orthotopic mouse model was more suitable as it could better reproduce clinical patient tests 12 , 13 . Thus, we established the orthotopic lung cancer C57 mouse model to further verify the promoting effect of taurine and proline on lung cancer (Fig. 2A ). Compared with the control and model group, taurine and proline both significantly increased body weight loss (Fig. 2B ). Similarly, taurine and proline not only increased the number of tumour lesions, but also significantly changed the original shape of the thoracic cavity in micro-CT images, compared with the model group (Fig. 2C, D ). Moreover, taurine and proline significantly increased lung tumour weight and lung/body ratios (Fig. 2E, F ). Together, these results provided in vivo evidence that taurine and proline had a significant tumour-promoting potency, indicating a poor prognosis for lung cancer. To further examine the mechanisms underlying the tumour-promoting potency of taurine and proline, we performed RNA-seq using orthotopic lung tumours. RNA-seq analysis revealed a total of 66 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in the proline-treated group compared to the model group. Among these, 44 DEGs were upregulated, while 22 showed downregulation (Fig. 3A and Supplementary Fig. 1A ). A total of ten down-regulated DEGs were found in the taurine-treated group compared to the model group (Fig. 3B and Supplementary Fig. 1B ). By further comparing the gene expression profiles of the proline-treated group, the model group, and the control group from the above RNA-seq data, we obtained 4 DEGs, namely C-X-C Motif Chemokine Ligand 9 (Cxcl9), Z-DNA Binding Protein 1 (Zbp1), the 3-Hydroxy-3-Methylglutaryl-CoA Synthase 2 (HMGCS2), and Azgp1 (Fig. 3C ). Four DEGs, including Azgp1, CD3 Delta Subunit Of T-Cell Receptor Complex (Cd3d), CD8 Subunit Alpha (Cd8a), and cytochrome P450 family 2 subfamily d polypeptide 10 (Cyp2d10), were also identified among the taurine-treated group, the model group, and the control group from the RNA-seq data (Fig. 3D ). Interestingly, we found for the first time that Azgp1 was co-down-regulated in both proline- and taurine-treated groups compared to the model group, indicating that Azgp1 may play a vital role in our findings. To verify whether our findings have the clinical significance, we examined Azgp1 expression in human LUAD and LUSC transcriptome dataset from the TCGA. Consistent with our findings, Azgp1 was both down-regulated in LUAD and LUSC tumours compared with normal lung tissues (Fig. 3E, F ). Also, the similar expression of the other DEGs were showed in patients with lung cancer compared to our findings (Supplementary Fig. 2 ). Moreover, lung tumours with low Azgp1 expression correlated with poor survival (Fig. 3G ), which was consistent with the reported results 21 . Therefore, low expression of Azgp1 gene in lung tumour suggests poor prognosis for lung cancer.

Taurine is a conditionally essential nutrient for humans and mainly involved in taurine and hypotaurine metabolism in vivo 22 , 23 . Proline is a unique proteinogenic secondary amino acid and mainly participates in arginine and proline metabolism 14 . We then performed spearman correlation analyses to further verify the correlation between Azgp1 expression and key targets of the taurine and proline metabolism pathways. In our results, Azgp1 expression was significantly correlated with key targets in taurine and hypotaurine metabolism, including Gamma-glutamyltransferase 1 (GGT1), Flavin Containing Dimethylaniline Monoxygenase 5 (FMO5), Gamma-glutamyltransferase 5 (GGT5), Flavin Containing Dimethylaniline Monoxygenase 2 (FMO2), Flavin Containing Dimethylaniline Monoxygenase 3 (FMO3), Cysteine Dioxygenase Type 1 (CDO1), Glutamate Decarboxylase-like Protein 1 (GADL1), and 2-aminoethanethiol Dioxygenase (ADO) (Supplementary Figs. 3 A–H and 4 ). And Azgp1 expression was also significantly correlated with key targets in arginine and proline metabolism, including Leucine Aminopeptidase 3 (LAP3), Prolyl 4-Hydroxylase Subunit Alpha 2 (P4HA2); Aldehyde Dehydrogenase 4 Family Member A1 (ALDH4A1), D-Amino Acid Oxidase (DAO), Proline Dehydrogenase 1 (PRODH), Pyrroline-5-Carboxylate Reductase 2 (PYCR2), Prolyl 4-Hydroxylase Subunit Alpha 1 (P4HA1), and Ornithine Decarboxylase 1 (ODC1) (Supplementary Figs. 3 I–P and 5 ). Therefore, Azgp1 was proved to be significantly associated with the taurine and proline metabolic pathways in lung cancer patients.

Azgp1, an adipokine synthesised by adipocytes and epithelial cells, not only acts as the cachexia related to cancer progression and cell cycle regulation, but also a critical regulator of lipid metabolism 24 , 25 . As an adipokine synthesised by adipocytes and epithelial cells, Azgp1 plays increasingly vital parts in metabolism-related diseases 26 . To investigate if the tumour-promoting effect of taurine and proline was related to the changes of lipid metabolism, we carried out a metabolome programme of orthotopic lung tumours.

In the comparison between model and control group, a total of 8586 and 2765 metabolites showed significant up-regulation and down-regulation, respectively (Fig. 4A, B, E ). Of these, 67 and 67 metabolites were obviously up-regulated and down-regulated between taurine and model group (Fig. 4A, C, F ). Three metabolites of MS2 were finally identified as lysoPC 16:3 (up-regulation), lysoPC 22:0 (down-regulation) and lysoPC 24:1 (down-regulation) (Fig. 4H, J and Supplementary Fig. 6 ). In the comparison between proline and model group, a total of 59 and 69 metabolites revealed distinct up-regulation and down-regulation, respectively (Fig. 4A, D, G ). Thereinto, 4 metabolites of MS2 were identified as PE (15:0/20:3(5Z,8Z,11Z)) (up-regulation), PC (18:3(9Z,12Z,15Z)/16:1(9Z)) (up-regulation), xanthosine (up-regulation), and uridine (down-regulation) (Fig. 4I, K and Supplementary Fig. 6 ). Moreover, the above 7 metabolites were mainly belonged to “lipids and lipid-like molecules”, followed by “nucleosides, nucleotides, and analogues”. What is more, the aberrant lipid metabolism is relevant to cancer development 27 , 28 . Therefore, taurine and proline may cause lipid metabolism disorder by down-regulating Azgp1 expression, and ultimately promote tumour growth. Fig. 4 Tumour-promoting effects of taurine and proline are closely associated with the alteration of lipid metabolism mediated by Azgp1. The metabolite profiles were generated by extracting and quantifying metabolites from lung tumours using UPLC-MS/MS across four groups: taurine (25 mg/kg, n = 3), proline (25 mg/kg, n = 3), model ( n = 3), and control ( n = 3). It has been reported that the anti-tumour effect of uridine was related to the coupling of taurine. Taurine is reported to form a conjugate with uridine, which could restore mitochondrial protein biosynthesis, strengthen mitochondrial function, and reduce superoxide generation 29 . The reduction of superoxide is known to inhibit tumour growth 29 , 30 . To investigate if the tumour-promoting effect of proline is due to impaired uridine regulation, LLC-xenografted C57 model mice were intervened with a combination of proline and uridine (Supplementary Fig. 7 ). In the results, compared with the model group, proline could notably promote lung tumour growth. However, the tumour-promoting effect of proline was obviously attenuated when combined with uridine. Taken together, these results indicate that proline could promote tumour growth by inhibiting the level of uridine in vivo.

As mentioned above, Azgp1 is a cachexia related to cancer progression and cell cycle regulation, as well as a critical regulator of lipid metabolism 24 , 25 . It was still unclear how taurine and proline affect lipid metabolism by inhibiting the Azgp1 gene, thereby promoting tumour growth. Literature research revealed a highly related protein kinase of mTOR. On the one hand, Azgp1 can affect fatty acid biosynthesis by inhibiting mTOR activity 31 , 32 . It is also reported that the PI3K/AKT/mTORC1/sterol regulatory element-binding protein (SREBP) pathway promotes cancer proliferation by inducing new lipid synthesis 33 . On the other hand, tumour cells need a lot of proteins, lipids, and nucleotides mediated by activated mTOR to meet their growth and differentiation needs 34 . Therefore, mTOR has been proved to play a key role in regulating metabolism and tumour growth. In metabolome analysis, more than half of the metabolites of MS2 were “lipids and lipid-like molecules,” followed by “nucleosides, nucleotides, and analogues” (Supplementary Fig. 8 ). GO enrichment (Supplementary Figs. 9 and 10 ) and KEGG pathways (Supplementary Figs. 11 and 12 ) also revealed that taurine and proline could induce the changes of lipid metabolism mediated by mTOR.

To further dissect the regulatory mechanisms, GSEA was performed used to analyse the downstream pathways that Azgp1 may regulate in 1017 lung cancer samples from the TCGA. We found that Azgp1 was significantly correlated with lipid metabolic pathways in 1017 lung cancer samples from the TCGA (Fig. 5A–H ). We also examined mTOR expression in human LUAD and LUSC transcriptome dataset from the TCGA. Consistent with our findings, mTOR was both up-regulated in LUAD and LUSC tumours compared with normal lung tissues (Fig. 5I, J ). Moreover, taurine and proline could co-down-regulate Azgp1 expression, and co-up-regulate mTOR expression in the western blot results (Fig. 5K and Supplementary Fig. 13 ). Therefore, Azgp1 is significantly correlated with downstream lipid metabolic pathways mediated by mTOR. sections.discussion:
Lung cancer remains one of the most deadly-cancers worldwide due to high mortality and extremely low 5-year survival rates 1 , 35 . Consequently, preclinical research is increasingly important for providing scientific countermeasures for lung cancer diagnosis and treatment 36 – 38 . Among these, an ideal mouse model of lung cancer plays a critical role in effective diagnosis, biomarker discovery, and active drug screening and evaluation 36 – 38 . The orthotopic lung cancer mouse model is closer to clinical practice because tumours directly affect lung function 37 . Our previous study demonstrated that the orthotopic lung cancer mouse model is the most suitable model for clinical metabolomics research 13 . Therefore, we applied the orthotopic lung cancer mouse model to examine the role of specific metabolites in lung cancer progression.

Amino acid metabolism plays an important role in evaluating the occurrence and progression of cancer. As substrates for protein synthesis, sufficient amino acid supply is very important to maintain the proliferative power of tumour cells. Anabolic/catabolic dysregulation of amino acids has been recognised as metabolic regulators in support of tumour cell growth 39 . Many cancers have an increased requirement for specific amino acids and develop a reliance on exogenous supplies or upregulated de novo synthesis 40 . The role of amino acids in supporting cancer cell proliferation and combating therapy benefits from maintaining redox homoeostasis, modulating epigenetic modifications, and providing metabolic intermediates for energy production 41 , 42 . In tumour microenvironment, amino acid metabolism can also produce immunosuppressive or immune-enhancing effects by affecting the anti-tumour immune response 42 . Different cancer exhibit different amino acid metabolism, suggesting that these differences can be exploited for more efficient and precise target metabolism 43 . Likewise, there are not only differences but also similarities in the regulatory effects of different amino acids on the same cancer process.

Taurine, a conditionally essential nutrient for humans 22 , 23 , is involved in regulating osmotic pressure, coupling bile salt, stabilising membrane and anti-oxidation and anti-inflammation. Taurine has been reported to suppress potential invasion and metastasis, helping to evaluate the development of malignant tumours such as breast, bladder, and colorectal cancer 44 , 45 . In addition, taurine transporter and LncRNA taurine up-regulated 1 are able to promote proliferation, migration, and invasion of tumour cells in some cancers 46 – 48 . Regarding proline, a unique proteinogenic secondary amino acid, it has a variety of functions not achievable by other amino acids 14 . Proline is also involved in cancer metabolism and affects cancer progression 14 . Proline oxidase and proline accelerate tumour progression by inducing the expression of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and inflammatory genes, including CXCL1, LCN2, and IL-17C 14 . Taurine and proline are key metabolites closely linked to cancer, and their changes in vivo may serve as potential indicators for monitoring cancer progression. Our results found for the first time that taurine and proline both promoted subcutaneous (Fig. 1 ) and orthotopic (Fig. 2 ) lung tumour growth. Therefore, in-depth study of the common molecular mechanism of taurine and proline in promoting lung cancer progression will help to better understand the important role of amino acid metabolism in the pathogenesis, progression, and prognosis of lung cancer.

To strengthen the findings presented in Supplementary Fig. 3 , we investigated the associations between Azgp1 and key enzymes in the taurine and proline metabolic pathways, which are critical in lung cancer progression and metabolic regulation. In taurine and hypotaurine metabolism (Supplementary Fig. 3A–H ), the correlation between AZGP1 and key enzymes in the taurine pathway suggests a potential role in regulating redox balance and tumour suppression: (1) GGT1 and GGT5 (positively correlated with Azgp1): These enzymes are central to glutathione metabolism, maintaining antioxidant defenses and redox homoeostasis 49 . Increased GGT expression can promote ROS production, which, at controlled levels, can induce tumour cell death 20 , 50 . (2) FMO2, FMO3, and FMO5 (positively correlated with Azgp1): These enzymes, implicated in multiple cancers, influence health pathways like lipid, glucose, and cholesterol metabolism, which may impact cancer risk and prognosis 51 – 53 . For example, FMO3’s role in TMAO production affects lipid and glucose regulation, potentially influencing cancer progression indirectly 53 . (3) CDO1 and GADL1 (positively correlated with Azgp1): CDO1 is critical for cysteine metabolism, influencing redox balance and lipid metabolism 54 , while GADL1 contributes to antioxidant production, such as β-alanine, potentially protecting against oxidative stress 55 . (4) ADO (inversely correlated with Azgp1): High ADO levels are linked to tumour growth and poor outcomes in other cancers, indicating its tumour-promoting effects 56 . These associations suggest that Azgp1’s positive correlation with enzymes like GGT1, GGT5, FMO3, and GADL1 might contribute to antitumour activity by promoting redox regulation and cellular stability. In contrast, its negative correlation with ADO suggests that low ADO levels may help limit tumour-promoting mechanisms, aligning with AZGP1’s potential tumour-suppressive role.

In arginine and proline metabolism (Supplementary Fig. 3I–P ), Azgp1 also shows positive correlations with enzymes involved in protein metabolism and oxidative stress responses, further supporting its antitumour potential: (1) LAP3: This enzyme regulates amino acid turnover, affecting protein synthesis and signalling pathways critical for cell function 57 . LAP3’s positive correlation with Azgp1 suggests an alignment with antitumour activity, as reduced LAP3 levels are linked to cellular homoeostasis and increased mTORC2-mediated AKT phosphorylation 57 . (2) P4HA2 and DAO: P4HA2, activated by tumour suppressor P53, stabilises HIF-1α, contributing to ROS regulation and antitumour effects 58 , 59 , while DAO induces oxidative stress and apoptosis, further supporting Azgp1’s role in inhibiting tumour growth 60 . (3) PRODH: Involved in proline breakdown, PRODH has been targeted for anticancer therapies 61 , indicating that Azgp1’s correlation with PRODH may also be beneficial in tumour inhibition. Conversely, Azgp1’s negative correlations with tumour-promoting enzymes such as ALDH1A1, P4HA1, ODC1, and PYCR2 further highlight its potential role in suppressing lung cancer progression. ALDH1A1 and ODC1, in particular, contribute to a tumour-promoting microenvironment, with high expression levels linked to poor prognosis 62 , 63 . P4HA1’s association with metastasis highlights the significance of Azgp1’s negative correlation with this enzyme 64 , suggesting that Azgp1 may help limit aggressive tumour characteristics. The enzymes pyrroline-5-carboxylate reductase (PYCR), which catalyzes the final step in proline biosynthesis, have been extensively linked to the progression of various malignancies 61 . This analysis supports the hypothesis that Azgp1 modulates lung cancer progression by influencing taurine and proline metabolic pathways. Genes positively correlated with Azgp1 may facilitate antitumour functions through redox balance and metabolic stability, while those negatively correlated may support tumour progression and survival.

Transcriptomics is a large-scale research method targeting RNA molecules that helps better understand numerous molecular underpinnings and biological processes for cancer 9 . It can provide correlations between cellular phenotypes and their molecular basis. Metabolomics can provide abundant information on cellular metabolic processes for tumour progression and serve as accurate biomarkers reflecting upstream biological events, such as gene mutations and environmental changes 6 , 7 . However, metabolomics alone is still not enough to identify more novel metabolic markers and further explain the related in vivo mechanisms, especially the associated upstream targets 65 . Therefore, the integration of metabolomic profiling with transcriptomics data can help fully understand the regulation process behind various physiological phenomena of biomarkers 11 .

In this study, we performed RNA-seq using orthotopic lung tumours to further explore the mechanisms underlying the tumour-promoting effects of taurine and proline. We found, for the first time, that Azgp1 was co-down-regulated in both proline- and taurine-treated groups compared to the model group (Fig. 3C, D ). Azgp1 is an important gene expressed in secretory cells of lung epithelium and plays a vital role in cancer progression and cell cycle regulation 66 . Consistent with our findings, Azgp1 expression is proved to be down-regulated in human LUAD and LUSC tumours compared with normal lung tissues from TCGA (Fig. 3E, F ). Moreover, low Azgp1 expression in tumours predicts poor survival for patients with lung cancer 21 . These findings indicate that taurine and proline may promote tumour growth by down-regulating Azgp1 expression.

Azgp1, known as Zinc-α2-glycoprotein, functions as an adipokine and plays important roles in regulating lipid metabolism, cancer-related cachexia, and cell cycle control 24 , 25 . Within the context of lung cancer, our study demonstrated that Azgp1 downregulation correlated with increased tumour growth (Figs. 1 – 3 ), partly because of its effects on lipid metabolic pathways (Fig. 4H, I and Supplementary Figs. 8 – 12 ). Specifically, the suppression of Azgp1, particularly in response to taurine and proline, disrupted lipid metabolism and enhances lung tumour proliferation. Our study highlighted that Azgp1 modulates lipid metabolism by influencing the mTOR pathway. Normally, Azgp1 downregulation reduces its inhibitory effect on mTOR, which in turn activates pathways that promote lipid synthesis 31 , 32 . This activation facilitates a metabolic environment favourable for cancer cell growth, as tumour cells require a steady supply of lipids for membrane synthesis, energy storage, and signalling. The mTOR pathway, particularly through the PI3K/AKT/mTOR/SREBP signalling cascade, induces de novo lipid synthesis, directly supporting cancer proliferation by providing essential lipids for rapidly dividing cells 33 . Metabolomic analysis revealed that taurine and proline treatments led to significant alterations in lipid metabolites, with observed upregulation and downregulation in various lipid molecules (Fig. 4 and Supplementary Figs. 8 – 11 ). For instance, lysoPC 16:3 was found to be upregulated, while lysoPC 22:0 and lysoPC 24:1 were downregulated in the taurine-treated group. Similarly, proline treatment affected additional lipid molecules, including phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) and phosphatidylcholine (PC), which are essential components of cell membranes and play key roles in signalling pathways. Moreover, taurine and proline can down-regulate protein Azgp1 and up-regulate protein p-mTOR (Fig. 5K ). These changes were significant because the altered levels of lipids and lipid-like molecules align with increased cancer cell survival and growth demands.

To further validate Azgp1’s role, the study overexpressed Azgp1 in lung cancer cells, observing a marked reduction in cell proliferation (Fig. 6 ). In vivo experiments also demonstrated that Azgp1 overexpression led to the inhibition of lung tumour growth in mouse models, suggesting a protective role for Azgp1 against lung cancer. Additionally, in these models, overexpressed Azgp1 was associated with decreased phosphorylation of mTOR, indicating that high Azgp1 levels can mitigate the mTOR pathway’s activation and subsequently curb lipid synthesis, reducing the metabolic support needed for tumour growth. In conclusion, Azgp1 affects lipid metabolism significantly by modulating the mTOR pathway.

Our results demonstrated for the first time that taurine and proline potentially promoted lung tumour growth, indicating a poor prognosis for lung cancer. We have for the first time identified a novel mechanism of the tumour-promoting effects of taurine and proline through an innovative integration of tumour metabolomics and transcriptome analysis. We ultimately proposes the Azgp1/mTOR axis as a key mechanism by which taurine and proline promote lung cancer (Fig. 7 ). Azgp1 downregulation releases its inhibitory effect on mTOR, thereby promoting mTOR-driven lipid synthesis pathways. This lipid metabolic shift, in turn, supports enhanced tumour proliferation and survival, illustrating a novel mechanism by which amino acids (taurine and proline) contribute to lung cancer progression through metabolic reprogramming. Therefore, our findings help provide a scientific basis for the pathogenesis, progression, and prognosis of lung cancer. Undeniably, we still lack further mechanistic evidence especially clinical results to confirm our results. In the future, we will integrate more clinical data and multi-omics studies to enrich our findings and better serve clinical practice.
